statement: Eleven identical cookies are shared among $4$ children, Ava, Ben, Cy and Dot, so that every cookie is given out, each child gets at least $1$ cookie, and no child gets more than $4$ cookies. In how many ways can this be done?

choices.misconception: I only listed the different sets of amounts, like 4, 4, 2, 1, and did not count which child gets which amount.
I counted the ways where some child gets more than 4 cookies, 4 times C(6, 3) = 80, and gave that instead of subtracting it from 120.
I gave each child 1 cookie and shared the other 7 freely, C(10, 3) = 120, but forgot the limit of 4 cookies per child.
I forgot both rules and counted every way to share 11 cookies among 4 children, C(14, 3) = 364.

hints: Hand every child 1 cookie first. Then 7 cookies are left, and each child may get at most 3 more.
Without the limit, sharing 7 cookies among 4 children is a stars and bars count. Then remove the shares where some child gets 4 or more extra cookies.

C(10, 3) = 120 shares in all. If one child gets at least 4 extra, give that child 4 and share the other 3 freely: C(6, 3) = 20 ways, for each of the 4 children. Two children cannot both get 4 extra. So 120 - 80 = 40.

solutions.reliable: Give each child $1$ cookie first. Now $7$ cookies remain, and each child may receive at most $3$ more. Without the limit, the number of ways to share $7$ identical cookies among $4$ children is $\binom{7 + 3}{3} = 120$. A share breaks the limit when some child gets $4$ or more extra cookies, and two children cannot both do that, since $4 + 4 > 7$. If a particular child gets at least $4$ extra, hand that child $4$ and share the remaining $3$ freely: $\binom{3 + 3}{3} = 20$ ways. With $4$ choices of child, that is $80$ bad shares. The answer is $120 - 80 = 40$.
solutions.elegant: List the sets of amounts, each from $1$ to $4$, that add up to $11$: $\{4, 4, 2, 1\}$, $\{4, 3, 3, 1\}$, $\{4, 3, 2, 2\}$ and $\{3, 3, 3, 2\}$. Each of the first three has exactly two equal amounts, so it can be handed out in $\frac{4!}{2!} = 12$ ways, and the last can be handed out in $\frac{4!}{3!} = 4$ ways. The total is $12 + 12 + 12 + 4 = 40$.
